title: Biographical record; family background
description: Dale Anderson works through a biographical questionnaire with Mabel Louise Scribner, recording her maiden name Gamsby, her 1899 birth in Toronto, and her arrival in Idaho in 1924. She gives details about her parents, her sisters Mary and Dorothy, her husband Charles Harry Scribner, and their marriage in Spokane in 1924.

title: Husband's Forest Service career; children
description: Scribner describes her husband's career as a forest ranger until his 1952 retirement and his later self-employment in timber cruising and surveying. She names their three children, Bill, Gwen, and Sidney, gives their birthdates in Spokane, and outlines their careers in state recreation, laboratory work on the polio project, and highway engineering.

title: Photography work; hobbies; clubs; Skywatch service
description: Scribner tells of her training in photographic developing and her apprenticeship at Libby Arts Studio in Spokane before marriage. She describes her collections of thimbles, buttons, frogs, and mugs, her gardening, her many club memberships including the DAR and Rebekah Lodge, and her World War II Skywatch service that earned her an Air Force life membership.

title: Life narrative; Alberta homestead; one-room school; father's career
description: Scribner recounts her life story: born in Toronto, moving at age six to her father's Alberta homestead after two train wrecks, and attending a one-room school taught by her aunt with makeshift desks and slates. She tells how the family moved through Nelson, B.C., to Spokane in 1914, where her father's partner absconded with their money and he rebuilt his living selling small paintings door to door.

title: Courtship and marriage; ranger station life
description: Scribner describes meeting Charles Scribner on a hunting trip, their quick courtship, and marriage in 1924. She recalls life in Avery, having her children in Spokane, transfers to St. Maries, Thompson Falls during World War II, and the Red Ives ranger station, plus her father living with the family for eighteen years.

title: Rural versus urban life; community hospital; city culture
description: Scribner reflects on preferring small-town life for its friendliness and the personal care at the St. Maries community hospital under Dr. Rapp. She also recalls enjoying Spokane theater, concerts, and the Follies as a girl, visiting the Spokane Expo many times, and missing the Seattle World's Fair.

title: Raising children; changing times
description: Scribner compares her strict childrearing with modern parenting, noting she kept her children young longer and faced few severe problems, though drugs existed even in her youth. She observes that radio and television bring world events closer and believes the world will keep progressing.

title: Housing; camping, hunting and fishing
description: Scribner describes her housing over the years, from Forest Service log cabins in Avery and a summer shack with outdoor plumbing to a modern CCC-era home at Red Ives. She tells of her love of camping, fishing, and hunting, including sleeping in their bronco and her husband's moose hunting trips to Canada.

title: Naturalization and citizenship
description: Scribner explains her complicated route to naturalization in 1956, involving her father's citizenship, a mislaid alien registration card, and a missed chance at citizenship by marriage. She took a university citizenship course and passed her examination a year later.

title: Childhood games; sex-segregated schools; children's education
description: Scribner recalls childhood games such as skiing on barrel staves, riding an ox, and kick the can, and the strict segregation of boys and girls in Canadian schools. She discusses her children's schooling in St. Maries and Montana, Bill's Navy service and GI Bill education, and contrasts past and present expectations for teachers' education.

title: First radios and phonographs
description: Mabel Scribner recalls the first Atwater Kent radio at Avery, how the electrified Milwaukee Railroad caused static, and her family's early Victrola and Edison phonographs in Spokane.

title: Courtship, wedding, and the lightning storm at Red Ives
description: She tells of meeting her husband on a rabbit drive near Ritzville, marrying suddenly in her mother's parlor, and riding a horse twelve miles up to the Red Ives ranger station. She recounts the Buttes lookout being struck by lightning and Danny Warren coming to rescue her as she rode through the electric storm.

title: Expectations of marriage; children and grandchildren
description: She explains that she originally intended to be an old maid with cats and foster children until she met her husband and changed her mind. She discusses her three children, thirteen grandchildren, learning about childbirth from her mother, and each grandchild's schooling and plans, including one girl who wants to be a forest ranger.

title: Women's roles and satisfaction with life
description: She gives her view that women can do men's jobs but that mothers of young children belong at home, and that she does not interfere in her children's family lives. She says she would change nothing about her life and feels she has been rewarded for her sacrifices.

title: Recreation, travel, reading, and television
description: She describes club dinners, her husband's slide shows, travels through many states and national parks, her first airplane ride to Tennessee, and trips she still hopes to make. She lists her favorite books, a long roster of magazines, and the television game shows she watches.

title: Marriage partnership and why they live in St. Mary's
description: She portrays her husband as a silent, secure man with whom she talks over major decisions. She explains that Forest Service work brought them to Avery and St. Mary's, which they love for its fishing, hunting, and mild climate.

title: Gardening and food preserving
description: She describes dividing the garden with her husband, freezing produce instead of canning, and how they plant garlic in October under straw. She mentions unusual crops like Jerusalem artichokes and purple beans, and the loss of their little dog.

title: The Depression and the wars
description: She says the Depression cost them a salary cut and lost bank savings but little hardship thanks to their home and garden. She found the war years harder, grieves for young men sent to battle, and says the United States had no business in Vietnam.

title: Raising the children and teaching a daughter
description: She remembers gardening with the boys, playing cards and Monopoly with them, their model airplanes and wood carving, and sewing their clothes on a treadle machine. She taught her daughter needlework and cooking, and tells of her daughter's early mishaps baking bread and huckleberry pie.

title: Childhood homestead: the 1910 fire, dances, and train wrecks
description: She recalls her grandmother and aunts in the household, fighting the 1910 prairie fire with water from sloughs and gunny sacks, and a collie that alerted them to the burning haystack. She also describes country dances where children slept on coats and two childhood train wrecks, one near Winnipeg with seven brides aboard.

title: Life now compared with thirty years ago; travels in the South
description: She contrasts her comfortable retirement, their Bronco, and traveling with friends in motels rather than camping with earlier years of mortgaging the house to pay college tuition. She recounts visiting her daughter in Arkansas, Alabama, and Tennessee across the seasons, coping with Southern heat.
